story.t: Server on-call today. Nobody has broken in yet, but a Linux server goes down on its own too: full disk, a service that won't start, memory running out.
I don't even need to attack. I'll wait for the disk to fill up and the kernel to kill your database for me.
df, systemctl, journalctl, free. The server talks, I just need to know how to ask.

levels.title: Permissions as numbers
levels.goal: Connect each numeric permission to what it allows.
levels.z: chmod 777 on everything and done. Fast, practical and great for me.
levels.me: Each digit is owner, group and others. Only allow what's needed.
lesson: Each file has permissions for the owner, the group and others, in that order.
As numbers: r = 4 (read), w = 2 (write), x = 1 (execute). Add them up: 6 = rw, 5 = rx, 7 = rwx, 4 = r only, 0 = nothing.
On a directory, x is the right to enter it. That's why a directory is usually 755 or 700.
A fourth digit in front turns on special bits: 4 is setuid, the program runs with the file owner's permission.
levels.tip: Read digit by digit: owner, group, others. 6 = rw, 5 = rx, 4 = r, 0 = nothing. The 4 in front of 4755 is setuid.
levels.learn: 644 for a regular file, 600 for a secret, 755 for directories and scripts, 700 for a private folder like ~/.ssh, 640 for a config the service's group reads and 4755 for setuid programs like passwd.

left.why: 644: the owner reads and writes, group and others only read. It's the standard for a regular file, like the site's index.html.
600: only the owner reads and writes. It's right for a secret, like the private key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.
755: the owner does everything, group and others read and enter or execute. Standard for directories and public scripts.
700: only the owner enters, reads and writes. SSH expects ~/.ssh like this.
640: the owner reads and writes, the group only reads, others nothing. Good for a config with a password read by the service's group.
4755: the 4 in front is setuid. The program runs with the owner's permission, like /usr/bin/passwd, which belongs to root.

right.t: Everyone reads, only the owner changes
right.why: Everyone reads and only the owner writes: 6 for the owner, 4 for group and others, 644.

right.t: Only the owner reads and writes
right.why: Only the owner with read and write: 6 for the owner, 0 for the rest, 600.

right.t: Everyone enters, only the owner changes
right.why: Entering a directory needs x: 7 for the owner and 5 (r + x) for group and others, 755.
Only the owner with everything and nobody else: 7 and two zeros, 700.
Owner rw (6), group r only (4), others nothing (0): 640.
Running with the owner's permission is setuid, the 4 in the fourth digit: 4755.

levels.title: Full disk in the middle of the night
levels.goal: Find out what filled app01's disk and free up space without taking the application down.
levels.intro: The order system stopped writing and the log shows No space left on device. Investigate app01.
levels.z: I didn't even need to break in. A forgotten log did the job for me.
levels.me: df to see what filled up, du to find the culprit.
lesson: df -h shows the usage of each filesystem. du shows how much each folder takes.
Deleting with rm a file a process still has open doesn't free space: the disk is only freed when the process closes the file. lsof +L1 shows these deleted but still open files.
truncate -s 0 empties the file without deleting it, and the space comes back immediately even with the process writing to it.
logrotate rotates and compresses logs. With copytruncate, it copies and empties the file, for programs that don't reopen their log on their own.
levels.tip: /var/log/app has a 31G debug.log because logging was left on DEBUG. Empty it with truncate (rm won't free it while Java has the file open) and create a logrotate rule.
levels.learn: DEBUG logging filled the disk with a 31G file. truncate freed the space without stopping the application, and logrotate with maxsize, compress and copytruncate keeps it from happening again. And rm on an open file frees nothing: lsof +L1 shows the ghost file.

cmds.why: / (root, /dev/sda2) is at 100% with no free space. Used shows 38G of 40G because ext4 reserves about 5% for root.
du adds up each folder's size. Of /var's 35G, 32G are in /var/log: they're logs.
A single file, debug.log, is 31G. It's still being written (current time).
Someone turned DEBUG mode on for a test and forgot. DEBUG records every detail and generates gigabytes a day.
The java process (PID 1432) has the file open for writing (5w). That changes the right way to free the space.

v: Who's to blame for the disk at 100%?
From what you investigated, what took up the space?
o: The application's debug.log, at 31G, because of DEBUG logging

o.why: /var/cache has 1.4G: tiny next to /var/log's 32G.
/boot/efi is another partition, at 1% use. It doesn't affect /.
/var/lib has 1.2G. What grew was the log.

steps.why: df showed / at 100%, du pointed to /var/log and ls found the 31G debug.log, generated by log_level on DEBUG.

steps.q: How do you free space now without stopping the application?
v: What's the safe way to get the space back right away, with the system running?
How do you empty that log without taking the order service down?

o.why: java keeps the file open: with rm the name goes away, but the space only comes back when the process closes the file. df would stay at 100%.
It frees the space, but takes the order system down and doesn't fix the cause: the log grows again.
The journal isn't to blame and it holds the system logs that help investigate.

steps.why: truncate zeroes the size of the file the process keeps using. The space comes back immediately and the application keeps writing to the same file.

steps.q: A colleague had already run rm on a big log and df didn't change. How do you find that file?
v: Someone deleted a log with rm and the space didn't come back. Which command shows the file?
The space didn't come back after an rm. How do you find the deleted file still using the disk?
o: sudo lsof +L1, which lists deleted files still open by some process

o.why: du only adds up files that still have a name. The deleted file doesn't show up, which is why df and du disagree.
The name was already removed from the directory: ls no longer shows the file.
fsck checks the filesystem structure. It's not for this, and running it with the disk mounted is risky.

steps.why: lsof +L1 shows files with zero links (no name) still open, marked (deleted). Restarting the owning process or truncating via /proc/PID/fd frees the space.

steps.q: And so it doesn't fill up again?
v: How do you keep the disk from filling up again?
What's the permanent fix?
o: Set logging back to INFO and create a logrotate rule with a max size, compression and copytruncate

o.t: Schedule an rm of the log every night
o.why: rm on an open file doesn't free space, and you lose the whole history at once.
It only delays it: with DEBUG logging, 80G fill up too.
Without logs, the next problem has no clues to investigate.

steps.why: The cause is the DEBUG level. logrotate caps the size, keeps a few compressed copies and, with copytruncate, works with programs that don't reopen the log file.

levels.title: Nginx won't start
levels.goal: Find out why nginx won't start on web02 and bring the site back up.
levels.intro: After yesterday's maintenance, web02 rebooted and the site didn't come back. nginx won't start.
levels.z: Someone installed a package yesterday. Just one package. Guess what came with it?
levels.me: systemctl status and journalctl. The reason is in the log.
lesson: systemctl status shows whether the service is active and the result of the last attempt. journalctl -u shows the service's log.
Two things can't listen on the same port and address. The Address already in use error means another process took the port.
systemctl stop stops the service now. systemctl disable keeps it from starting at boot. disable --now does both.
apt also installs dependencies and recommended packages, marked as automatic. The history lives in /var/log/apt/history.log.
levels.tip: The journal says port 80 is already in use. ss shows apache2 on it, installed along with libapache2-mod-php. Disable apache2 and start nginx.
levels.learn: apache2 came along with libapache2-mod-php, started at boot and took port 80 before nginx. With disable --now on apache2, nginx starts. For PHP with nginx, the way is php-fpm.

cmds.why: The config test (ExecStartPre, nginx -t) passed, but ExecStart failed. The configuration is fine: the problem is at startup.
bind() failed with Address already in use: another process is already listening on port 80.
What's on port 80 is apache2, another web server.
nginx's configuration is valid. Touching it wouldn't help.
Yesterday someone installed libapache2-mod-php8.3, which is PHP for Apache. apache2 came along, marked as automatic.

v: What stops nginx from starting?
What's causing nginx to fail?
o: Port 80 is already taken by another process

o.why: nginx -t and ExecStartPre passed: the configuration is valid.
A firewall filters incoming connections. It doesn't stop a service from listening on the port.
The status shows enabled: it tried to start and failed.

steps.why: The log shows bind() failed (98: Address already in use). Only one process can listen on the same port and address.

steps.q: Who took port 80 and how did it get there?
v: Who's on port 80 and where did it come from?
Which process is on 80 and why is it installed?
o: apache2, which came along yesterday with the libapache2-mod-php8.3 install

o.why: The process is apache2, and apt's history shows it was installed by a team member.
ss shows apache2 on port 80, not nginx.
php8.3-mysql is just PHP's database extension. It doesn't listen on any port.

steps.why: ss shows apache2 on 80, and history.log shows apache2 marked as automatic in the libapache2-mod-php8.3 install. At boot, it started before nginx.

steps.q: How do you bring the site back up the right way?
v: What's the fix to get nginx back?
What do you do so the site comes back with nginx?
o: Disable apache2 with disable --now and start nginx (PHP on nginx goes through php-fpm)

o.why: The site would leave the standard port and visitors wouldn't arrive. The right move is removing what shouldn't be on 80.
apache2 is still enabled: it comes back on the next boot and the problem repeats.
nginx is fine (nginx -t passed). The port is what's taken.

steps.why: disable --now stops apache2 now and keeps it from starting at boot. With the port free, nginx starts. PHP for nginx is php8.3-fpm, not the Apache module.

steps.q: Why wasn't systemctl stop apache2 enough?
v: What's the problem with just stopping apache2 with stop?
Why use disable and not just stop?
o: stop only lasts until the next boot: apache2 stays enabled and starts again

o.t: stop doesn't really stop the process
o.why: stop does stop the service. The problem is it comes back at boot.
stop doesn't delete anything, it just stops the service.

o.t: It was enough, there's no difference
o.why: There is: it was exactly the boot that brought apache2 back to port 80.

steps.why: enable and disable control boot. start and stop control now. disable --now does both: stops now and no longer starts at boot.

levels.title: Who killed the database?
levels.goal: Find out who took down loja01's MySQL and keep it from happening again.
levels.intro: At the peak of the sale, the online store started showing database connection errors. The site and MySQL run on the same server, loja01.
levels.z: I didn't touch your database. Your own kernel pulled the trigger.
levels.me: If it was the kernel, it's recorded in dmesg.
lesson: When memory runs out, the kernel triggers the OOM killer (out of memory) and kills a process to save the system.
It picks by oom_score, which mainly weighs how much memory each process uses on its own. The one that dies is usually the biggest process, not the culprit.
In free -h, the column that matters is available: free memory plus the cache the kernel can release.
php-fpm runs one process per concurrent request. pm.max_children limits how many can exist at the same time.
levels.tip: dmesg shows the OOM killer killing mysqld. What filled the memory were dozens of php-fpm processes of ~175 MB each, allowed by pm.max_children = 100. Lower the limit so it fits in RAM.
levels.learn: The high pm.max_children let php-fpm open 40 processes of ~175 MB at the peak, memory ran out and the OOM killer killed the biggest single process, mysqld. Limiting php-fpm to what fits in RAM protects the database.

cmds.why: Only 96Mi left in available, and there's no swap. The server is out of memory.
The kernel logged it: Out of memory, killed process 1187, mysqld, which was using about 2.5 GB (anon-rss).
systemd confirms Result: oom-kill and tries to restart MySQL. With no memory, it goes down again.
The top of the list is all php-fpm, each at about 175 MB (RSS) and 2.2% of memory. Alone, none is scary. Together, it depends on how many there are.
41 processes: the master and 40 workers. 40 × 175 MB is about 7 GB, almost all of the 7.7 GB RAM.
pm.max_children = 100 allows up to 100 workers. At 175 MB each, that'd be 17 GB on a 7.7 GB server.

v: What took MySQL down?
Who ended the database process?
o: The kernel's OOM killer, because memory ran out

o.why: dmesg records Out of memory: Killed process. It was the kernel, no attacker.
It wasn't a MySQL crash: systemd shows Result: oom-kill, death from lack of memory.
systemd only tries to start it again after the kernel killed the process.

steps.why: With no memory available and no swap, the kernel triggers the OOM killer and kills a process so the whole system doesn't freeze.

steps.q: free shows 118Mi under free. Which column really says how much is still usable?
v: Which free column shows the memory that can really still be used?
To know whether memory is short, which free column do you look at?
o: available, which adds free memory and the cache the kernel can release

o.why: free ignores the cache, which the kernel gives back when needed. On a healthy server, free is usually low anyway.
used shows what's taken. For the headroom, look at available.
shared is shared memory (tmpfs and the like), not the system's headroom.

steps.why: Linux uses spare memory as disk cache. available estimates how much can be allocated without swap. Here it's only 96Mi: memory really is short.

steps.q: If php-fpm filled the memory, why did the kernel kill mysqld?
v: Why did the OOM killer pick MySQL and not php-fpm?
php-fpm filled the memory. Why was the database the victim?
o: The OOM killer picks by oom_score, which weighs each process's memory: mysqld was the biggest on its own

o.t: Because MySQL is the oldest process
o.why: Process age doesn't decide. The criterion is oom_score, based mostly on memory.
The user doesn't protect the process. What counts is each one's memory.

o.t: The kernel always kills the database first
o.why: The kernel doesn't know what a database is. It looks at each process's oom_score.

steps.why: Each php-fpm has about 175 MB, and mysqld alone had 2.5 GB. php-fpm's combined memory caused the problem, but the victim was the biggest single process.

steps.q: What's the fix so the database stops going down?
v: How do you avoid another OOM at the next peak?
What do you tune so the database doesn't die again?
o: Limit php-fpm to what fits in RAM (pm.max_children = 20) and reload the service

o.t: Raise pm.max_children to serve more people
o.why: More workers means more memory: the OOM would come even faster.
The database keeps dying at the peak, it just comes back sooner.

o.t: Kill the php-fpm processes whenever memory climbs
o.why: It drops customer requests and doesn't fix the configuration.

steps.why: With about 3.5 GB set aside for PHP and ~175 MB per worker, about 20 fit. Extra requests wait in the queue instead of taking the database down.

levels.title: Cron schedule
levels.goal: Read the cron schedules and find out why the backup isn't running.
levels.z: I changed one comma in your crontab. Your backup now runs... someday.
levels.me: Five fields: minute, hour, day, month and day of week.
lesson: A cron line has 5 time fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, then the command.
* = any value. */15 = every 15. In day of week, 0 and 7 are Sunday.
In a user's crontab -e, the command comes right after the 5 fields. In /etc/cron.d/, a column with the user who runs it comes first.
cron runs with a minimal environment (short PATH, no .bashrc of yours). Use the full path in commands.
levels.tip: Read field by field: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. /etc/cron.d has the user column. A script that works by hand and fails in cron is almost always PATH.
levels.learn: cron's 5 fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. In /etc/cron.d the user goes before the command, cron runs with a minimal environment and the execution log lives in the cron service's journal or in syslog.

v: The line 0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh runs when?
At what time does 0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh run?

o.why: Every 3 minutes would be */3 * * * *. Here 0 is the minute and 3 is the hour.
00:03 would be 3 0 * * *. The first field is the minute.
Day of month is the third field, which here is *.

qs.why: Minute 0, hour 3, any day, any month, any day of week: every day at 03:00.

v: How often does */15 * * * * run?
A task at */15 * * * * runs when?
o: Runs every 15 minutes (00, 15, 30 and 45 of every hour)

o.why: 3 p.m. would be 0 15 * * *. The */15 is in the minute field.

o.t: Runs on the 15th of every month
o.why: The 15th would go in the third field: 0 0 15 * *.
*/15 in the minute field is 4 times an hour, 96 a day.

qs.why: */15 in the minute field means every 15 minutes: 0, 15, 30 and 45.

v: The schedule 30 2 * * 0 runs when?
On which day and time does 30 2 * * 0 run?

o.why: That would be 30 2 * * *. The last field, 0, limits it to Sunday.
Monday is 1. In day of week, 0 and 7 are Sunday.
Day of month is the third field, here *. The 30 is the minute.

qs.why: Minute 30, hour 2, day of week 0: Sunday at 02:30. Sunday can be written 0 or 7.

qs.q: Which line in /etc/cron.d/backup runs the backup as root on the 1st of every month at 04:00?
v: In /etc/cron.d/backup, which line runs as root on every 1st, at 04:00?
Which /etc/cron.d entry schedules the backup for the 1st of the month, 04:00, as root?

o.why: In /etc/cron.d the user column is missing. Without it, cron reads the script path as a user name.
Minute 4, hour 0: runs at 00:04, not 04:00.
The 1 in the fourth field is the month: it'd run every day in January at 04:00.

qs.why: Minute 0, hour 4, day of month 1, any month, any day of week, user root and the command with its full path.

qs.q: backup.sh works when you run it by hand, but fails in cron. What's the most common cause?
v: A script runs in the terminal and breaks in cron. What is it usually?
Why does a script that works by hand fail when cron runs it?
o: cron runs with a minimal environment: short PATH and none of your shell's variables

o.why: cron runs any command or script with execute permission.

o.t: cron only runs while the user is logged in
o.why: cron runs with nobody logged in. That's what it's for.
cron uses the system time zone. A wrong time doesn't make the script fail.

qs.why: In the terminal you have your PATH and your .bashrc. In cron, PATH is short (something like /usr/bin:/bin). Use full paths or set PATH at the top of the crontab.

qs.q: Where do you confirm whether cron ran the backup?
v: How do you check whether the cron task ran?
Which command shows cron runs on Ubuntu?

o.why: crontab -l only lists what's scheduled, not what ran.
backup.sh isn't a systemd service. cron is what runs it.
Shows the system schedule, not the run log.

qs.why: On Ubuntu and Debian, cron logs each run in the cron service's journal and in syslog, with the command's CMD line.
